C005.subject: Class size reduction to below 18 students
C005.object: reading achievement scores more than math achievement scores
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Class size reduction to below 18 students reading achievement scores more than math achievement scores]

[PATH:empirical] Project STAR (Tennessee Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio) longitudinal data reanalysis focusing on differential effects by subject (reading vs. math) and by poverty status — Project STAR is the largest randomized controlled trial on class size reduction. A targeted reanalysis of its K-3 data, particularly for high-poverty subgroups, can directly test whether reading gains exceed math gains when class sizes are below 18.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of class-size reduction studies (e.g., from the What Works Clearinghouse or Hattie's Visible Learning) that report separate effect sizes for reading and math achievement in early elementary grades — A systematic synthesis of existing studies can quantify and compare the average effect sizes for reading vs. math, especially in high-poverty contexts, and assess whether the differential effect is consistent across studies or an artifact of specific designs.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of instructional time allocation and cognitive load in smaller classes: how reduced class size may differentially affect decoding/ comprehension (reading) vs. procedural skills (math) in early grades — Developing or leveraging an existing cognitive-educational theory can explain mechanisms (e.g., more individual feedback for reading, which is more language-dependent and interactive) and generate testable predictions to guide empirical work.

scope.domain: early elementary grades (K-3) with high-poverty student populations

C006.subject: Class size reduction
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Class size reduction educational outcomes]

[PATH:empirical] Tennessee Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) project longitudinal data — This large-scale randomized experiment (1985-1989) directly tests class size reduction effects on K-3 outcomes; re-analysis of its long-term follow-up can confirm or refute whether initial gains persist or fade, addressing the disputed claim.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of class size reduction studies (e.g., Hattie's Visible Learning or meta-analyses by Finn & Achilles) — A systematic synthesis of multiple studies provides aggregate effect sizes and identifies moderators (e.g., socioeconomic status, teacher quality) that explain when and why class size reduction may not improve outcomes, directly evaluating the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Economic cost-effectiveness analysis comparing class size reduction to alternative interventions (e.g., tutoring, teacher training) — A theoretical framework comparing marginal benefits per dollar spent can show whether class size reduction's effect is too small to be educationally meaningful, refuting its improvement claim even if statistically significant.

C007.subject: Class size reduction in secondary grades (9-12)
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Class size reduction in secondary grades (9-12) educational outcomes for low-achieving students]

[PATH:empirical] Tennessee STAR follow-up studies: Analyze long-term outcomes for low-achieving students in reduced vs. regular-size secondary classes, focusing on graduation rates and test scores. — The STAR experiment is a landmark randomized trial; secondary-grade follow-ups can directly test whether class size reduction worsens outcomes for low achievers.

[PATH:empirical] California Class Size Reduction (CSR) program evaluation data: Examine subgroup effects for low-achieving 9-12 students using state longitudinal records. — California's large-scale CSR implementation provides quasi-experimental variation; focusing on low-achieving subgroups can reveal whether negative effects emerge due to resource dilution or peer effects.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of class size effects by Hattie (2009) and subsequent updates: Re-analyze moderator effects for secondary grades and student ability levels. — Existing meta-analyses often average effects; a targeted re-analysis for low-achieving secondary students can identify if the hypothesis is supported or contradicted by cumulative evidence.

C008.subject: Class size reduction
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Class size reduction educational outcomes]

[PATH:empirical] Tennessee's Student Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) project reanalysis with modern causal inference methods (e.g., instrumental variables, difference-in-differences) focusing on secondary grades 9-12 — The STAR experiment is a landmark randomized study on class size, but its original findings were for early grades. Reanalyzing long-term outcomes for secondary students using updated econometric techniques could directly confirm or refute the hypothesis for grades 9-12 in the U.S.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of class size reduction studies in U.S. high schools (1990–2025) from the What Works Clearinghouse or similar systematic review databases — A comprehensive meta-analysis specific to secondary grades would synthesize existing evidence, controlling for publication bias and heterogeneous effects, providing a robust test of the disputed hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental analysis of state-level class size reduction mandates (e.g., California's Class Size Reduction program) using administrative data on high school graduation rates and standardized test scores — Natural experiments from policy changes in the U.S. since the 1990s offer exogenous variation in class sizes. Analyzing these with regression discontinuity or panel data methods can isolate causal effects on educational outcomes for grades 9-12.

C009.subject: Class size reduction
C009.object: targeted small-group interventions for students two or more grade levels behind
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Class size reduction targeted small-group interventions for students two or more grade levels behind]

[PATH:empirical] Tennessee STAR (Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio) longitudinal dataset reanalysis focusing on students initially two or more grade levels behind, with subgroup effect sizes compared to small-group tutoring interventions (e.g., from the National Student Support Accelerator). — Directly compares the marginal benefit of class-size reduction versus targeted small-group interventions for the specific subgroup of low-performing students, addressing the hypothesis in a resource-constrained K-12 setting.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials on high-dosage tutoring (e.g., Nickow, Oreopoulos, & Quan, 2020) versus meta-analyses of class-size reduction (e.g., Hattie, 2009; Krueger, 2003), with a focus on effect sizes for students two or more grade levels behind. — Synthesizes existing evidence to compare average effect sizes across intervention types, controlling for dosage and student baseline, thereby testing whether targeted small-group interventions outperform general class-size reduction for the stated population.

[PATH:theoretical] Simulation-based cost-effectiveness analysis modeling resource allocation in a typical U.S. school district (e.g., using the Cost-Effectiveness Analysis in Education framework), comparing per-pupil costs and achievement gains of reducing class size by 5 students versus implementing small-group pull-out tutoring for struggling students. — Provides a theoretical comparison under resource constraints, clarifying whether the hypothesized effectiveness gap holds when accounting for fixed budgets and opportunity costs, which is central to the domain specified.

C010.subject: targeted small-group interventions
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: targeted small-group interventions universal class size reduction]

[PATH:empirical] Tennessee STAR (Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio) experiment re-analyses post-2000 — This landmark randomized controlled trial provides direct evidence on class size reduction effects. Re-analyses focusing on subgroup outcomes (e.g., low-income or at-risk students) can be compared with targeted small-group intervention studies to assess relative effectiveness.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analyses of targeted small-group interventions (e.g., reading or math pull-out programs) in US K-12 settings since 2000 — Systematic reviews and meta-analyses (e.g., from What Works Clearinghouse or Campbell Collaboration) synthesize effect sizes across many studies. Comparing these effect sizes with those from class size reduction studies (e.g., STAR) can directly test the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Cost-effectiveness analysis comparing targeted interventions vs. universal class size reduction — Even if effect sizes differ, policy decisions depend on cost per unit of student gain. A theoretical model incorporating costs, implementation fidelity, and scalability can clarify whether the hypothesis holds under realistic constraints.
